content: 1. HIV-positive individuals are those who have tested positive for the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), indicating the presence of the virus in their body. 2. HIV-negative individuals are those who have tested negative for HIV, meaning they do not have the virus. This group may include mothers who have ceased breastfeeding. 3. For individuals with an unknown HIV status, outcomes may include death, loss to follow-up, transfer to another facility, or other scenarios. 4. Program records are used to directly measure the final outcome status of HIV-exposed infants. These records also assess the quality of the program in terms of follow-up care until the final HIV status of the infant is determined. 5. Co-trimoxazole (CTX) prophylaxis coverage measures the percentage of HIV-exposed infants who begin CTX prophylaxis within two months of birth. This intervention reduces the risk of opportunistic infections and bacterial infections in these infants. 6. The percentage of HIV-positive women of reproductive age (15–49 years) attending HIV care and treatment services who have unmet needs for family planning is an indicator of whether their family planning needs are being addressed to prevent unintended pregnancies. 7. Seroconversion among pregnant women refers to the percentage of initially HIV-negative pregnant women who are retested during pregnancy and found to have become HIV-positive. This measures the effectiveness of efforts to prevent HIV transmission to uninfected pregnant women. 8. Testing coverage of male partners of pregnant women attending antenatal care (ANC) measures the percentage of male partners tested for HIV during the pregnancy. Identifying serodiscordant couples is critical for preventing HIV transmission to both the pregnant woman and her partner. 9. The turnaround time for early infant diagnosis (EID) results measures the percentage of EID test results returned within four weeks of specimen collection. Timely return of results is essential for initiating appropriate care and treatment. 10. The six-week mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) rate measures the percentage of infants born to HIV-positive women who are HIV-positive at six weeks of age. This indicator evaluates efforts to reduce peripartum HIV transmission. 11. Infant antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation measures the percentage of identified HIV-positive infants who start ART by 12 months of age. This is a critical quality-of-care indicator, as early ART initiation reduces mortality risk in HIV-infected infants. 12. Early retention rates measure the percentage of pregnant or breastfeeding women on ART who remain on treatment at one and three months after initiation. High retention rates indicate program success and quality, as women are most likely to drop out shortly after starting ART. 13. Coverage of baseline CD4 counts or clinical assessments in ANC measures the percentage of HIV-positive pregnant women assessed by CD4 count or clinical staging at ART initiation. This clinical assessment is recommended to guide treatment decisions. 14. The percentage of HIV-positive pregnant women who deliver in a health facility measures the program’s ability to ensure that these women access prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) services during delivery. 15. The rate of preterm births (<37 weeks gestation) among HIV-positive women who received ART and delivered within the past 12 months is monitored. A higher-than-expected rate may indicate the need for further assessment of national policies on ART use during pregnancy. 16. The number of new pediatric HIV cases due to MTCT is an impact indicator for validating the elimination of mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT) of HIV. Investigating each case is essential to understand the reasons for transmission. 17. Mortality measurement is a key indicator of national program success in scaling up HIV prevention, treatment, and care. A decrease in HIV-related mortality reflects the effectiveness of the health sector response. 18. In the absence of complete civil registration systems, facility-based mortality surveillance, verbal autopsies, and other methods can be used to measure HIV-related mortality. These approaches require careful analysis and extrapolation to ensure data quality and representativeness. 19. Verbal autopsy (VA) involves interviewing family members or close friends about the circumstances surrounding a death to determine the cause. This method is commonly used in settings without reliable civil registration data. 20. Sample vital registration with verbal autopsy (SAVVY) systems provide a cost-effective alternative to full national civil registration systems for collecting accurate mortality data. 21. National-level HIV-related mortality can also be measured by adding VA to general population surveys or including it in prospective cohort studies. 22. High-quality interviewers and well-trained coders are essential for a valid VA system. Simplified algorithms using key signs and symptoms can help identify HIV-related causes of death. 23. Measuring the impact of HIV programs requires linking outcomes, such as preventive behaviors and treatment, to changes in HIV incidence and mortality. This evaluation is critical for understanding the contributions of interventions and improving the health sector response.
